docs.title: Website Development
docs.text:
Welcome to the website development lesson hub.

In these lessons, you will plan, design, build, test, and improve websites for different projects. Each project may have a different theme, audience, and purpose, but the same design process will help you make clear and useful pages.

You will learn how to:

  • Plan a website for a specific audience
  • Organise information into clear sections
  • Design wireframes before building
  • Create pages with a consistent layout
  • Test and improve your work
  • Explain the choices you made

docs.title: How to Use These Lessons
docs.text:
Work through each lesson in order. The activities will guide you from early planning to a finished website.

Most lessons include:

  • Learning intention and success criteria
  • Keywords
  • Examples
  • Levelled tasks
  • Reflection questions

Use the navigation menu to choose your current project and lesson.

docs.title: Visit Edinburgh
docs.text:
Welcome to the Visit Edinburgh website development unit.

In this unit, you will plan, design, build, test, and evaluate a one-page website about Edinburgh. Your website should help a chosen audience find useful information before visiting the city.

You will use RocketCake to build the website, so the focus is on good design choices rather than writing code.

docs.title: Unit Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the unit, you will create a one-page website called Visit Edinburgh.

Your work will be judged using this rubric:

Skill Area Level 1 Beginning Level 2 Making Progress Level 3 Making Good Progress Level 4 Meeting Target Planning Basic audience or purpose is recorded Audience and purpose are identified with a simple plan Clear audience, purpose and section plan Detailed plan explains why each section suits the audience and purpose Research Limited facts are recorded or sources are missing Some useful facts are recorded with at least one source Useful facts are recorded with sources for text and images Facts are well chosen, rewritten, and linked to user needs Website Build Page is incomplete or difficult to follow Page has some useful content, headings or images One-page RocketCake site has title, sections and images Page is polished, visually consistent and easy to scan Information Structure Some content is present but weakly organised Content is grouped into simple sections Content is organised into logical sections Structure helps users compare information quickly Testing Limited checking Some checks are completed and one improvement is made Tests are completed and fixes are recorded Testing includes peer, accessibility, and device checks, with improvements recorded Evaluation Simple opinion Evaluation describes at least one strength and one improvement Evaluation explains strengths and improvements Evaluation explains strengths and improvements using evidence and computing vocabulary

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text: Skill What This Means Planning Decide the audience, purpose, sections, and order of your page before building. Research Find useful information and record where it came from. Information Structure Organise information into clear sections so visitors can find and compare information easily. Design Create a wireframe so you know where headings, text, images, and sections will go. Website Build Use RocketCake tools to create a clear one-page website. Testing Check that your website is readable, accessible, and suitable for visitors. Evaluation Explain what worked well and what you improved.

docs.title: Website Theme
docs.text:
Your website should help a specific audience explore Edinburgh. Some pupils may design a general visitor guide, while others may focus on a particular type of visit.

You might choose an audience such as:

  • tourists and first-time visitors
  • football or rugby fans
  • theatre audiences
  • music fans
  • people attending concerts or festivals
  • families looking for activities
  • visitors who need transport, accessibility, or safety information

Your sections should match your audience. For example, a sports fan website might include stadium information, transport, food nearby, and match day tips. A theatre or music website might include venues, event information, travel options, food nearby, and accessibility details.

You do not need to include every idea. Choose the sections that best support your audience and purpose.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Think about these questions:

  1. Who is the website for?
  2. What will your audience need to know first?
  3. Which Edinburgh information will be most useful?
  4. How can images make the page more helpful?
  5. How will you know if your website helps your audience successfully?

docs.title: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Plan a one-page website by identifying the audience.
  • Plan the purpose of the website.
  • Choose useful sections for the page.
  • Decide the order of the content before building.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • I can identify the target audience and the website's main purpose.
  • I can choose useful sections for a design.
  • I can explain why the section order helps the visitor.
  • I can create a clear page plan before building.

docs.title: Todays Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Audience Who the website is designed for, such as tourists, families, or first-time visitors. Purpose What the website is trying to do, such as inform, guide, persuade, or help someone plan. Section A block of related content on the page, such as attractions, transport, or visitor tips. Information The facts, details, and messages the visitor needs. Layout How text, images, headings, and sections are arranged on the page.

docs.title: Before You Plan the Page, Plan the Visitor's Journey
docs.text:
When you are designing a website you should always be thinking of the end user and asking:

Question What to Think About Who is it for? Choose a specific audience, such as families, tourists, students, or first-time visitors. What does the user need? Think about the visitor's main goal, such as planning a trip, finding attractions, or checking transport. What information comes first? Put the most useful details near the top so visitors do not have to search for them. What action should the user take? Decide whether the site guides the visitor to explore, book, contact someone, or plan their route.

Each question helps you decide what the visitor needs and how the page should be organised.

The order of sections is important because visitors usually look at the top of a page first. Important information should appear before less important details.

docs.title: Using Clear Headings
docs.text:
Headings help visitors understand what each section is about.

Good headings:

  • Clearly describe the content below them
  • Help visitors find information quickly
  • Break a page into easy-to-read sections
  • Make the website easier to navigate

Examples:

  • Top Attractions
  • Getting Around Edinburgh
  • Places to Eat
  • Visitor Tips

docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

docs.title: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Learn what a wireframe is used for.
  • Plan the sections for a one-page website.
  • Decide where headings, text, and images could go.
  • Create a wireframe before building the website.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • I can explain what a wireframe is used for.
  • I can choose suitable sections for my website.
  • I can place sections in an order that helps the visitor.
  • I can add clear notes about headings, text, and images.

docs.title: Todays Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Wireframe A simple plan that shows where the main parts of a web page will go. Section A block of related content on the page, such as attractions, transport, or visitor tips. Heading A short title that tells the visitor what a section is about. Content Order The sequence that information appears in on the page. Annotation A short note added to a design to explain what should be included.

docs.title: Designing a Wireframe
docs.text:
Every website needs a clear visitor journey. Before we start building, we create a simple plan showing how the page will be organised.

In Web Development this is called a Wireframe.

A wireframe does not need finished colours, fonts, or images. It is a planning tool that helps you decide what each section will contain before you start building.

Wireframes help designers spot problems before they start building. Making changes to a wireframe is much quicker than rebuilding a finished website.

When creating your wireframe, think about:

  • What the visitor needs first
  • Which sections will be most useful
  • Where headings, text, and images could go
  • How the page will guide the visitor from top to bottom

docs.title: Designing for Your Audience
docs.text:
Different audiences may need information in a different order.

For example:

  • Tourists may want attractions near the top of the page.
  • Families may want visitor tips and facilities.
  • First-time visitors may need transport information.
  • Returning visitors may be more interested in events and activities.

Your wireframe should be organised to meet the needs of your chosen audience.

docs.title: What Is an Annotation?
docs.text:
An annotation is a short note added to a wireframe.

Annotations help explain:

  • What text will go in a section
  • What image could be used
  • What heading should appear
  • Any important information the visitor needs

Annotations make it easier for someone else to understand your design.

docs.title: Example Layout
docs.text:
This is one possible section order for the Visit Edinburgh website.

Section Purpose Title A strong heading and image to welcome visitors. Introduction A short overview of what the page is about. Attractions Key places to visit in Edinburgh. Transport How to get to and around the city. Visitor tips Practical advice for a better trip. Credits Sources, image credits, and extra information.

The order matters because visitors should see the most useful information before they reach smaller details such as credits.

docs.title: Wireframe Checklist
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure your wireframe has space for:

  • A clear page title
  • A short introduction
  • At least three useful content sections
  • Notes for headings
  • Notes for text
  • Notes for images
  • Credits or source information

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Use your answers from Task One to decide the sections, headings, and order of your website.

Start at Level One then keep working through the questions.

Challenge yourself to see how far you can go.

Level OneLevel TwoLevel ThreeLevel FourChallenge Question

Create a basic wireframe and add sections in an order that mostly makes sense.

Create a clear wireframe with suitable sections in a sensible order, with notes for headings, text, and images.

Create a detailed wireframe and add well-chosen sections in a logical order that guides the visitor.

Create a complete wireframe and add all key sections in the best order, with clear notes so someone else could build the page.

Justify your section order by linking it to the audience's needs.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain what a wireframe is.
  • Describe why a wireframe is useful before building.
  • Choose suitable sections for a Visit Edinburgh website.
  • Explain why your section order helps the visitor.
  • Add clear notes so someone else could understand your design.

docs.title: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Find useful facts for a one-page website.
  • Choose reliable sources for text and images.
  • Record where information and images came from.
  • Organise research using an information model.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • I can find useful facts from suitable sources.
  • I can explain why a source is reliable.
  • I can record sources for text and images.
  • I can organise research using the same fields for each item.

docs.title: Todays Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Source Where information or an image came from, such as a website, map, guide, or official page. Reliable Information that is accurate, trustworthy, and suitable for the task. Information Model A structured way to describe real-world things using the same set of fields. Characteristic A detail that describes an item, such as its name, location, or description. Source URL The web address that shows exactly where your text or image came from.

docs.title: Good Research Helps Visitors
docs.text:
When building a website, you should not just collect lots of facts. You should choose the information that helps the visitor most.

For the Visit Edinburgh website, the audience is tourists who want useful trip information quickly. This means your research should be:

  • Relevant to the visitor
  • Easy to understand
  • From a trustworthy source
  • Recorded clearly so you can use it later

When researching, ask yourself:

Question What to Think About Is the source suitable? Check if the website is relevant, current, and likely to be trustworthy. What fact is useful? Choose details that would help a visitor plan or enjoy their visit. Can I rewrite it? Put facts into your own words so your website is clear and original. What source is needed? Save the website name and URL so you can show where your information came from and find it again later if needed.

docs.title: Why Record a Source?
docs.text:
Recording sources is an important part of research.

When you record the source URL, you can:

  • Find the information again later
  • Check that the information is accurate
  • Show where your research came from

When you record where an image came from, you can:

  • Find the image again if needed
  • Check that it is suitable for your website
  • Give credit to the original source

Good research is not collecting everything. It is choosing what helps the visitor.

docs.title: Choosing a Reliable Source
docs.text:
Not all websites are equally trustworthy.

Reliable websites often:

  • Belong to official organisations or businesses
  • Are regularly updated
  • Provide accurate contact information
  • Have clear, professional content
  • Match information found on other trusted websites

For a tourism website, official visitor, museum, council, and attraction websites are usually more reliable than websites with unusual names, excessive advertisements, or unclear ownership.

docs.title: Why Source Quality Matters
docs.text:
The quality of your sources affects the quality of your website.

Reliable sources help visitors trust your information and make good decisions when planning a visit.

Poor sources may contain mistakes, outdated information, or misleading facts. Using unreliable sources can make a website less useful and less professional.

Good websites are built using good research.

docs.text:

Start at Level One then keep working through the task.

Question 4

Question 7

docs.title: Using an Information Model
docs.text:
An information model helps you organise research in a clear and consistent way.

Each column in an information model is called a field.

A field stores one type of information, such as:

  • Name
  • Description
  • Location
  • Source Type
  • Source URL

Every row should contain information for the same fields.

The fields in an information model are often used to store characteristics of an item, such as its name, location, description, or category.

If you describe each attraction or visitor topic using the same fields, the information becomes easier to:

  • Compare
  • Sort
  • Search
  • Reuse in your website

You can think of this like a research table. The headings go across the top, then you add a new row for each attraction or visitor topic.

Here is an example with two attractions:

Name Description Location Source Type Source URL Edinburgh Castle Historic castle with exhibitions, views, and Scottish history. Castlehill, Edinburgh Text https://www.visitscotland.com/ National Museum of Scotland Museum with science, history, design, and nature exhibits. Chambers Street, Edinburgh Image https://www.nms.ac.uk/

This makes the information easier to understand because you can clearly see what to write in each column and add more rows as you continue your research.

Using the same fields for each item makes it easier for visitors to compare attractions and find useful information quickly.

docs.title: What Makes Information Useful?
docs.text:
Good information should be:

  • Accurate
  • Relevant to the visitor
  • Clear and easy to understand
  • Detailed enough to be helpful

For example:

❌ Edinburgh Castle – A castle.

✅ Edinburgh Castle – Historic castle with exhibitions, city views, and important Scottish history.

The second example gives visitors more useful information and helps them decide whether they would like to visit.

A complete information model normally contains multiple rows, with one row for each attraction, location, service, or topic you want to include on your website.

docs.title: Task Two
docs.text:
Use your website plan and wireframe to design an information model for the Visit Edinburgh website.

Start at Level One then keep working through the questions.

Challenge yourself to see how far you can go.

Level OneLevel TwoLevel ThreeLevel FourChallenge Question

Create a complete information model with SEVERAL rows of data that match your website topic and are purposeful and informative.

Explain how your information model helps someone collect and compare information quickly.

docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain what a source is.
  • Describe why reliable sources matter.
  • Record sources for text and images.
  • Explain what an information model is.
  • Use the keywords source, reliable, information model, characteristic, and source URL correctly.

docs.title: Answering Describe Questions
docs.text:
This page is here to help you answer describe questions in Computing Science.

A describe question asks you to say what something is like.

docs.title: What Does Describe Mean?
docs.text:
A describe question asks you to give details about something.

When you describe, you should:

  • Say what it is
  • Give important details
  • Use clear Computing Science words
  • Avoid giving a very short answer

A describe answer does not always need a reason. It mainly tells the reader what something is like.

Possible Describe Sentence Starters

You could start a describe answer with:

  • A source is...
  • A reliable website has...
  • An information model contains...
  • The source URL shows...
  • A field stores...
  • A characteristic is...
Example 1Example 2Example 3 Part Example Question Describe what a source is. Weak Answer A source is a website. Why This Is Weak This answer is too short. A source can be a website, but it does not give enough detail. Better Answer A source is where information or an image originally came from. It could be a website, map, guide, book, or official page. When building a website, sources are used to collect facts and images that help the visitor. Why This Is Better Says what a source is, gives examples of sources, and links the answer to the website task. Part Example Question Describe what an information model is. Weak Answer It is a table. Why This Is Weak This answer is partly correct, but it does not explain what the table is used for or what it contains. Better Answer An information model is a structured way of organising information about real-world things. It usually uses fields, such as name, location, description, source type, and source URL. Each row stores information about one item, such as one visitor attraction. Why This Is Better Says what an information model is, mentions fields, gives examples of fields, and links the answer to the Visit Edinburgh website task. Part Example Question Describe one sign that a website source is trustworthy. Weak Answer It looks good. Why This Is Weak This answer is too vague. A website looking good does not always mean the information is reliable. Better Answer One sign that a website source is trustworthy is that it belongs to an official organisation, such as a council, museum, visitor attraction, or tourism website. Official websites are more likely to contain accurate and useful information. Why This Is Better Gives a clear sign of trustworthiness, gives examples of official organisations, uses the word accurate, and links the answer to tourism research.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain what a describe question is asking you to do
  • Give clear details in your answer
  • Use Computing Science vocabulary correctly
  • Add examples when they help your answer
  • Describe what something is like without needing to explain why

docs.title: Answering Explain Questions
docs.text:
This page is here to help you answer explain questions in Computing Science.

An explain question asks you to give a reason why something matters, happens, or is useful.

docs.title: What Does Explain Mean?
docs.text:
An explain question asks you to give a reason.

When you explain, you should:

  • Make a clear point
  • Give a reason why
  • Add detail to show understanding
  • Use words such as because, so, therefore, or this means that

An explain answer should not just say what something is. It should help the reader understand why it matters.

Possible Explain Sentence Starters

You could start an explain answer with:

  • This is important because...
  • This helps because...
  • This means that...
  • As a result...
  • The reason for this is...
  • This would improve the website because...
Example 1Example 2Example 3 Part Example Question Explain why facts should be rewritten in your own words. Weak Answer So you do not copy. Why This Is Weak This answer gives a small reason, but it does not explain the reason clearly enough. Better Answer Facts should be rewritten in your own words because copying directly from a source can make the website less original and harder to understand. Rewriting facts helps you show that you understand the information. It also lets you make the text clearer and more suitable for your own website audience. Why This Is Better Uses the word because, gives more than one reason, links the answer to the final website, and explains how rewriting helps the audience. Part Example Question Explain why recording the source URL is important. Weak Answer So you know where it came from. Why This Is Weak This answer is on the right track, but it needs more detail. Better Answer Recording the source URL is important because it shows exactly where the information came from. This means the information can be checked again later to make sure it is accurate. It also helps prove that the research came from a suitable source rather than being guessed or copied without care. Why This Is Better Gives a clear reason, explains why checking later is useful, links source recording to accuracy, and shows why careful research matters. Part Example Question Explain why the quality of your sources affects the final website. Weak Answer Because bad sources are bad. Why This Is Weak This answer repeats the question and does not give a proper reason. Better Answer The quality of sources affects the final website because reliable sources help make the information accurate and trustworthy. If poor sources are used, the website may include mistakes, outdated facts, or misleading information. This could make visitors trust the website less and make the website less useful. Why This Is Better Explains the impact of reliable sources, explains the problem with poor sources, links source quality to visitor trust, and shows how research affects the final product.

docs.title: Describe or Explain?
docs.text: Command Word What It Means What Your Answer Should Do Describe Say what something is like Give details and examples Explain Give reasons why something matters or happens Use because, so, therefore, or this means that

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain what an explain question is asking you to do
  • Use words such as because and this means that
  • Give a clear reason in your answer
  • Add enough detail to show understanding
  • Explain why something matters, is useful, or happens
